edits.after_excerpt: 3.1 Under the Countable Choice convention in [F1], the periodic targets are separable. Consider finite vector Fourier arrays with coefficients in $\mathbb Q+i\mathbb Q$, support in $\{|k|_\infty\le N\}$ for an integer $N$, and conjugate symmetry; their associated real polynomials form a countable family. For $H$ and $V$, apply $P_k$ to each coefficient. This preserves conjugate symmetry and gives finite solenoidal arrays; $P_0=I$ retains the mean mode. Given a target field, first truncate its coefficient series in its target norm, then approximate the finitely many coefficients by rational real and imaginary coordinates with the opposite modes paired by conjugation. Since $P_k$ is a contraction and fixes the target solenoidal coefficients, the projected rational approximants converge in the $H$ or $V$ norm. For the real $H^{-r}$ space, omit the projections: its definition as the weighted completion of finite conjugate-symmetric arrays gives the same density argument. Complex targets use the corresponding unpaired rational complex arrays. Thus every periodic target named here is separable; [F2] supplies the bounded-domain targets under its own Axiom of Choice hypothesis. Finally, $L^p_{\rm loc}$ is exactly the conjunction of the Bochner-class conditions over finite intervals. No stronger assumption on the abstract spaces in the Definition is needed. [given, F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

edits.after_excerpt: Keep the actual map $z:[0,T]\to H$ defined by its limiting coefficients at every time. Define a separate $V$-valued representative $\widetilde z(t)=z(t)$ where the gradient square sum is finite and $\widetilde z(t)=0$ on the exceptional null set. The continuous finite-dimensional maps $\Pi_Mz$ converge to $\widetilde z$ in $V$ almost everywhere, so $\widetilde z$ is strongly measurable. Its $V$ norm is integrable in square because the integrated $H$ norm is at most $TA^2$ and the integrated gradient square sum is at most $B$. Thus $\widetilde z$ defines a class in $L^2(0,T;V)$ whose $H$-valued class is represented by the unchanged weakly continuous map $z$. The asserted pointwise $H$ bound and every limiting Fourier coefficient continue to refer to that unchanged map; only the Bochner representative has been assigned zero on the exceptional set.

Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\widehat{a_i a_j}(k)|\le\|a_i\|_2\|a_j\|_2$, hence the Euclidean tensor norm of this coefficient is at most $C_d\|a\|_2^2$. edits.after_excerpt: 1.1 Put $w_k=(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^r$. For any sequence $c$ with $\sum_kw_k^{-1}|c_k|^2<\infty$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\sum_kc_k\cdot\widehat\varphi(-k)|\le\|c\|_{H^{-r}}(\sum_kw_k|\widehat\varphi(-k)|^2)^{1/2}$. Repeated integration by parts bounds the last factor by a constant times $p_M(\varphi)$ for an integer $M>r+d/2$, because smooth Fourier coefficients decay as $(1+|k|)^{-M}$. Thus the displayed pairing is absolutely convergent and continuous, so defines a periodic distribution; testing on one character recovers each $c_k$, proving injectivity. It agrees with the regular distribution of an $L^2$ field by Fourier truncation and Parseval. Since $\|P_k\|\le1$, coefficient multiplication by $P_k$ is a contraction on $H^{-r}$, preserves real conjugate symmetry, and agrees on $L^2$ with the supplied projection. Now $a_i a_j\in L^1$ and Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\widehat{a_i a_j}(k)|\le\|a_i\|_2\|a_j\|_2$, hence the Euclidean tensor norm of this coefficient is at most $C_d\|a\|_2^2$. The unprojected divergence coefficient is $b_k=i\sum_j\kappa_{k,j}\widehat{a_{\cdot}a_j}(k)$ and has size at most $C_d|\kappa_k|\|a\|_2^2$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]
